name: Second Spanish Republic
info: The democratic republic that governed Spain from the deposition of King Alfonso XIII in 1931 until its defeat by the Nationalist rebels of General Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War in 1939.

facts.founder: The republican parties of the Pact of San Sebastián; Niceto Alcalá-Zamora headed the provisional government
facts.predecessor: The monarchy of King Alfonso XIII (the dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera had fallen in 1930)
facts.successor: The Nationalist regime of Francisco Franco; a Republican government in exile survived until after the restoration of democracy in Spain

t: The Republic was proclaimed on 14 April 1931, two days after republicans won a landslide in the municipal elections, and King Alfonso XIII went into exile.
The Constitution of 1931 ended Catholicism's status as the state religion, allowed divorce, extended the vote to women and gave every region the right to autonomy.
A military uprising on 17 July 1936 began the Spanish Civil War, in which an estimated half a million people died, and the Republic was dissolved on 1 April 1939.
dyk: In the Revolution of 1934 the miners of Asturias, in the towns they held, officially declared a proletarian revolution and abolished regular money; the rising lasted two weeks before the army crushed it.
ev: Two days after the municipal elections, the Second Republic is proclaimed and King Alfonso XIII goes into exile
The new Constitution, drafted by a Constituent Cortes, comes into force in December
Catalonia is granted autonomy, with a parliament and a president of its own
The Spanish Confederation of the Autonomous Right (CEDA) wins the elections, opening the "black biennium"
The entry of three CEDA ministers into the government sets off the Revolution of 1934, crushed in Asturias by the army
The Popular Front wins the general election of 16 February
An army uprising in Spanish Morocco on 17 July begins the Spanish Civil War
Madrid falls in March, and the Republic is dissolved after surrendering to the Nationalists

sections.foundation:
On 28 January 1930 the military dictatorship of General Miguel Primo de Rivera, in power since September 1923, was overthrown. Republicans of many backgrounds, conservatives, socialists and Catalan nationalists among them, joined forces in the Pact of San Sebastián, which committed them to overthrowing the monarchy and allowed a joint campaign against it. The municipal elections of 12 April 1931 gave the republicans a landslide victory. Two days later the Second Republic was proclaimed, King Alfonso XIII went into exile, and a provisional government was formed under Niceto Alcalá-Zamora. On 11 May Catholic churches and buildings in cities such as Madrid and Sevilla were set on fire.

In June 1931 a Constituent Cortes was elected to draft a constitution, which came into force in December. The Radical and Socialist majority then postponed regular elections for two more years, and the government of Manuel Azaña began numerous reforms in what it saw as a modernisation of the country. These two years are known as the Reformist Biennium. The Republic adopted the Himno de Riego as its national anthem and a tricolour of red, yellow and purple as the flag of Spain.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Republic's economy was mostly agrarian, and many historians call Spain in these years a "backward nation". Its major industries lay in the Basque region, which had Europe's best high-grade non-phosphoric ore, and in Catalonia, on the opposite side of the country from its resources, so that the mountainous terrain made transport very costly. Exports were low and manufacturing worked mainly for the home market. High levels of poverty left many Spaniards open to extremist parties.

The first governments carried out social reforms: a legal right to seven days of paid annual leave, the freedom to strike without fear of dismissal, new social security benefits and an eight-hour working day. A moderate agrarian reform expropriated landowners, and after the failed coup of the Sanjurjada it was made more radical against the aristocracy. In 1932 religious orders were forbidden to run schools while the government began a large school-building project. The Constitution allowed divorce, stripped the nobility of any special legal status and laid down procedures for nationalising public services, land, banks and railways. The land reforms were suspended in the "black biennium" that followed the elections of 1933.
sections.military:
The Republic faced armed risings from both sides. Monarchist generals planned the first coup against it, the Sanjurjada, which failed; several hundred generals were dismissed. An anarchist insurrection ended in the Casas Viejas massacre. In October 1934 the miners of Asturias occupied Oviedo, killing officials and clergymen, and mobilised thirty thousand workers within ten days. The rising was crushed after two weeks by the army under General Eduardo López Ochoa, known afterwards as the "Butcher of Asturias", which used mainly Moorish colonial troops from Spanish Morocco.

On 17 July 1936 General Franco led the Spanish Army of Africa from Morocco against the mainland while General Emilio Mola moved south from Navarre. Most of the main cities stayed loyal, and the rebels began a war of attrition. Fascist Italy, Nazi Germany and Portugal gave the rebels much greater and more effective help than the Soviet Union, Mexico and the International Brigades gave the Republic, while France and Britain kept to non-intervention. The Republicans held Madrid in November 1936 and at Jarama and Guadalajara in 1937, but the north fell in late 1937. The bombing of Guernica served as a testing ground for the Condor Legion, and the Battle of the Ebro in 1938 was the Republic's last attempt to turn the tide.
sections.governance:
The Constitution of 1931 created a single chamber, the Congress of Deputies, and guaranteed freedom of speech and association. It ended Catholicism's status as the state religion, and its articles 26 and 27 put strict controls on Church property and barred religious orders from teaching; scholars have called it hostile to religion, and Pope Pius XI condemned the deprivation of Catholics' civil liberties in the encyclical Dilectissima Nobis. Every region had the right to autonomy: Catalonia used it in 1932 and the Basque Country in 1936, while Galicia's statute never came into effect because of the war.

Politics was deeply divided. When the CEDA won the elections of 1933, President Alcalá-Zamora would not let its leader, Gil Robles, form a government and invited Alejandro Lerroux of the Radical Republican Party instead; the CEDA governed indirectly until it won three ministries in October 1934. The left regarded the CEDA as fascist, and Gil Robles praised Mussolini, Hitler and Dollfuss. After the Popular Front's victory in February 1936 Manuel Azaña formed a government and soon replaced Alcalá-Zamora as president. During the war the Republic had three governments, led by José Giral, Francisco Largo Caballero and Juan Negrín.
sections.impact:
The Republic's reforms touched the Church, the land, the regions and women's place in politics, and they divided Spain sharply. The Constitution opposed the key beliefs of a right wing rooted in rural areas and stripped the Church of its schools and public subsidies, while churches were burnt in 1931, 1932 and 1933. On the extreme right the Spanish Renovation, the small Falange Española and the Carlist militias grew; the historian Julián Casanova describes the anti-Republican right's culture as proto-fascist. Historians still disagree about the elections of February 1936: Stanley G. Payne and the scholars Manuel Álvarez Tardío and Roberto Villa García argue that there was major fraud, while Eduardo Calleja and Francisco Pérez reply that the Popular Front would have won a narrow majority even so.

The war that ended the Republic became an international event. Germany and Italy intervened for the rebels, the Non-Intervention Committee isolated the Republic, and the bombing of Guernica inspired Picasso's painting. In the Republic's territory a social revolution broke out after July 1936, inspired mostly by libertarian socialist, anarchist and communist ideas, with the trade unions of the UGT and the CNT as its main forces.
sections.decline:
The killing of the anti-fascist Lieutenant José Castillo by Falangist gunmen on 12 July 1936 was followed early on 13 July by the murder of the monarchist leader José Calvo Sotelo by Assault Guards and leftist militiamen; later investigations named the socialist gunman Luis Cuenca. Stanley Payne holds that the killing turned a faltering conspiracy into a revolt, and within hours Franco, who had stayed out of the plotting, committed himself to it. The coup began on 17 July. Bloody purges followed in every area the rebels captured. An estimated half a million people died in the war; some have put the figure as high as a million, but modern research gives 500,000.

After the north and the Aragon front fell and the Battle of the Ebro failed, Barcelona fell to the rebels in early 1939. The military coup of Segismundo Casado against Negrín ended Republican resistance, Madrid fell in March, and the Republic was dissolved on 1 April 1939 after surrendering to the Nationalists. Its government survived in exile, keeping an embassy in Mexico City until 1976, and formally dissolved itself after the restoration of democracy in Spain.

summary: The Second Spanish Republic governed Spain from 1931 to 1939. Its Constitution separated Church and state, gave women the vote and granted regional autonomy, but the reforms and the clashes between left and right split the country, and the military uprising of July 1936 began the civil war that ended with the Republic's surrender to Franco's Nationalists.
references: Antony Beevor, The Battle for Spain: The Spanish Civil War 1936–1939 (Penguin Books, 2006)
Julián Casanova, The Spanish Republic and Civil War (Cambridge University Press, 2010)
Stanley G. Payne, The Spanish Civil War (Cambridge University Press, 2012)
Paul Preston, The Coming of the Spanish Civil War: Reform, Reaction and Revolution in the Second Republic (Routledge, 1994)
Paul Preston, The Spanish Civil War: Reaction, Revolution and Revenge (HarperCollins, 2006)
Hugh Thomas, The Spanish Civil War (Harper & Row, 1977)

pointDescs.1931: The Republic is proclaimed on 14 April after the republicans' landslide in the municipal elections, and the Constitution comes into force in December.
pointDescs.1932: The Azaña government's reforms of the Reformist Biennium go ahead: Catalonia gains autonomy, religious orders lose their schools and a large school-building project begins.
pointDescs.1933: Azaña loses parliamentary support and President Alcalá-Zamora forces his resignation in September; the CEDA wins the November elections and the "black biennium" begins.
pointDescs.1934: Three CEDA ministers enter the government on 1 October, and the Revolution of 1934 is crushed in Asturias and Catalonia.
pointDescs.1935: A series of crises and the Straperlo and Nombela scandals weaken the governing parties, and President Alcalá-Zamora calls new elections.
pointDescs.1936: The Popular Front wins in February; after the murder of José Calvo Sotelo, the army uprising of 17 July begins the civil war.
pointDescs.1937: The Republicans turn back offensives at Jarama and Guadalajara, but the north, including the Basque Country, falls in late 1937.
pointDescs.1938: The Battle of the Ebro, from July to November, fails to turn the tide.
pointDescs.1939: Barcelona falls early in the year, the Casado coup ends resistance, Madrid falls in March and the Republic is dissolved on 1 April.

notes: The article gives no year for the Sanjurjada; I placed it only in the Azaña years, without a date.

'formally dissolved the following year' (after the restoration of democracy) is ambiguous in the article; I wrote only that the government in exile dissolved itself after the restoration of democracy.
